clinicalPearls: The adrenal has a rich arterial supply draining through a single central vein, creating a vascular dam that predisposes the medullary-cortical junction to haemorrhage under stress.
Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage typically presents non-specifically with abdominal, flank or back pain, fever and progressive hypotension, so acute adrenal crisis is easily overlooked.
Suspect it in any critically ill patient with unexplained shock that is refractory to fluids and vasopressors.
Antiphospholipid syndrome is the classic cause of spontaneous bilateral haemorrhage, and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia can drive adrenal vein thrombosis with subsequent bleeding.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome describes haemorrhagic adrenal destruction with disseminated intravascular coagulation, historically in meningococcal sepsis.
Neonatal adrenal haemorrhage follows difficult delivery or macrosomia and presents with a flank mass, prolonged jaundice and anaemia.
Unilateral haemorrhage usually preserves adrenal function, whereas bilateral involvement threatens Addisonian crisis and warrants empirical glucocorticoid before biochemical confirmation.
Hyponatraemia with hyperkalaemia, eosinophilia and hypoglycaemia should prompt urgent cortisol and ACTH testing.
reference.pathophysiology: The adrenal cortex receives a rich arterial supply from three separate arteries but drains through a single central vein, so any rise in venous pressure or intra-adrenal arterial flow produces stasis and rupture at the cortico-medullary junction. Physiological stress (sepsis, surgery, burns, trauma) drives an ACTH-mediated surge in adrenal blood flow while catecholamines and cytokines promote vasoconstriction and thrombosis of the small draining veins, culminating in haemorrhagic infarction. Prothrombotic and bleeding states amplify this, including antiphospholipid syndrome, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, anticoagulation and disseminated intravascular coagulation. When both glands are involved, destruction of cortical tissue produces acute primary adrenal insufficiency with combined glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency.
additionalDifferentials: haemorrhagic adrenal adenoma or adrenocortical carcinoma
additionalInvestigations: non-contrast and contrast-enhanced CT of the adrenals
adrenal MRI with in- and opposed-phase and gradient-echo sequences to characterise and date blood products
short Synacthen test with paired ACTH to assess adrenal reserve
plasma renin and aldosterone to confirm mineralocorticoid deficiency
antiphospholipid antibody panel and screening for heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
plasma or urinary metanephrines to exclude phaeochromocytoma
redFlags: haemodynamic instability or shock unresponsive to fluids and vasopressors
hyperkalaemia with hyponatraemia suggesting evolving adrenal crisis
reference.prognosis: Unilateral haemorrhage usually resolves with preservation of adrenal function, whereas bilateral haemorrhage causing acute insufficiency carries substantial mortality if crisis is unrecognised; survivors may recover partially or require lifelong hormone replacement.
pitfalls: attributing hypotension solely to sepsis and missing coexisting adrenal crisis
withholding glucocorticoid while awaiting confirmatory biochemistry
mistaking a contrast-enhancing haematoma for a solid tumour
failing to investigate an underlying antiphospholipid syndrome or heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
continuing anticoagulation without recognising the adrenal as the bleeding source
references: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on primary adrenal insufficiency
management: Treat suspected adrenal crisis immediately with parenteral hydrocortisone and intravenous fluid resuscitation without waiting for confirmatory tests
Provide long-term glucocorticoid and, where mineralocorticoid deficiency is confirmed, fludrocortisone replacement in bilateral disease causing adrenal insufficiency

Identify and treat the underlying cause such as sepsis, anticoagulation, antiphospholipid syndrome or heparin-induced thrombocytopenia, stopping heparin and using an alternative anticoagulant in the latter
Support haemodynamics and correct coagulopathy while balancing the competing risks of bleeding and thrombosis
Assess adrenal reserve with a short Synacthen test and paired ACTH once stabilised, and re-image to monitor resolution
Escalate to critical care for refractory shock, considering interventional or surgical control of ongoing haemorrhage
Reassess the need for lifelong hormone replacement, as some patients recover partial adrenal function
